title: Shinjuku Area Guide: What to Do in Tokyo's Busiest Hub
content:
Shinjuku is Tokyo at its most concentrated — a district that crams together neon nightlife, vast shopping, skyscrapers, and a beautiful park, all around one of the world's busiest train stations. It can be dizzying, so here's how to navigate it and what not to miss.

Unlike Asakusa's old-Tokyo character or Shibuya's youth-fashion pull, Shinjuku doesn't have a single identity — it's several districts stacked on top of each other, split cleanly by the station itself. That split is the easiest way to hold the area in your head: government towers and hotels to the west, department stores and daytime shopping to the east, and the nightlife strip of Kabukicho and Golden Gai just beyond that.

The station (don't panic)

Shinjuku Station is enormous and famously confusing — over 200 exits across a sprawling underground maze that connects JR lines, Tokyo Metro, and several private railways. The trick: know which exit you need before you arrive (follow signs to landmarks or compass directions — East Exit for Kabukicho and the department stores, South Exit for the bus terminal and newer developments, West Exit for the skyscraper district), and don't be afraid to just surface and reorient if you get turned around underground. Once outside, the district itself is entirely walkable and far less intimidating than the station beneath it.

What to do

  • Shinjuku Gyoen: one of Tokyo's loveliest parks, a genuinely serene escape with French, English, and Japanese formal gardens — gorgeous in cherry blossom season (late March–early April) and worth the small entry fee any time of year. Arrive early on weekends to beat the crowds.
  • Omoide Yokocho ("Memory Lane"): atmospheric lantern-lit alleys of tiny eateries and bars, most seating just a handful of people at a time — perfect for an early evening of yakitori and a beer before the crowds peak.
  • Golden Gai: a warren of minuscule themed bars, a Tokyo nightlife institution — many welcome visitors, some don't, and cover charges are common; a little research on a specific bar before you go smooths the experience.
  • Kabukicho: the big, brash entertainment district next to Golden Gai — vibrant and intense at night, with the giant illuminated Godzilla head over the Toho building as its unofficial mascot.
  • Skyscraper district & observation decks: the west side's cluster of towers includes free city views from government building observatories — a real money-saver next to paid options elsewhere in Tokyo.
  • Shopping: huge department stores (Isetan is the standout for its basement food hall alone), electronics megastores, and endless retail radiating out from every station exit.

Where it fits in your trip

Shinjuku is a top choice for where to book a hotel thanks to its transport links and all-in-one convenience — nearly every train line in Tokyo touches it, which matters more than almost anything else when you're basing a short trip in one spot. (This article contains affiliate links — if you book through them we earn a small commission at no extra cost to you.) It's also a top choice to go out at night. By day it's strong for shopping and the park; by night it's the heart of Tokyo nightlife. Many travelers pass through its station constantly regardless of where they stay, simply because so many connections run through it.

Eating in Shinjuku

Beyond Omoide Yokocho's yakitori stalls, Shinjuku rewards a little food planning: the basement food halls (depachika) under Isetan and the other department stores sell restaurant-quality bento and desserts for a fraction of a sit-down meal, ideal for a park picnic at Gyoen. Ramen options cluster around the East Exit, and Golden Gai's bars often serve a simple food menu alongside drinks if you want to combine the two. For a sit-down meal with a view, several of the skyscraper hotels on the west side have restaurant floors open to non-guests — a good option if you want Shinjuku's energy from a quieter vantage point.

Getting to and from Shinjuku

Shinjuku sits on the JR Yamanote loop line, so it connects directly to Tokyo Station, Shibuya, Ueno, and most of the city's other major hubs without a transfer — one of the reasons it works so well as a base. It's also the departure point for several long-distance highway buses, and the Narita Express runs directly here from Narita Airport (about 80 minutes), making Shinjuku one of the more convenient bases if you're flying into Narita rather than Haneda.

Practical tips

  • Use station lockers or your hotel to avoid hauling shopping around all day — Shinjuku's stores are numerous enough that bag fatigue sets in fast.
  • Trains stop running around midnight — plan your night accordingly, or budget for a taxi back if you're out late in Kabukicho or Golden Gai.
  • In Kabukicho at night, ignore touts offering to lead you to a bar or club — stick to venues you researched or found yourself.
  • The west side is skyscrapers and calm; the east side is shopping and nightlife — a useful mental map when you're deciding which direction to walk out of the station.

Bottom line

Shinjuku rewards a bit of fearlessness — embrace the energy, pick a couple of targets (the park by day, the alleys by night), and don't let the giant station intimidate you. It's Tokyo's beating heart and an essential part of the city, whether you base yourself here or just pass through.
excerpt: Shinjuku packs nightlife, shopping, parks, and the world's busiest station into one district. Here is how to make sense of it, plus where to eat and where to stay.

title: Shibuya & Harajuku Area Guide
content:
Shibuya and Harajuku sit side by side on Tokyo's west side and together form the city's youthful, fashion-forward heart. They're easy to combine into a single day of wandering, and the contrast between the two — electric energy giving way to boutique calm giving way to a forest shrine — is one of the best single-day snapshots of what makes Tokyo interesting. Here's what to see in each.

Shibuya

Shibuya is anchored by the world-famous Shibuya Crossing, the scramble intersection where up to 3,000 people surge across in every direction at once when the lights change. Walk it once at street level, then watch the spectacle from above — the Shibuya Sky observation deck and the window seats at the Starbucks overlooking the crossing are both popular vantage points, though Sky charges admission and the Starbucks is first-come, first-served. Nearby is the Hachiko statue, a beloved meeting spot named for a dog famous for waiting at the station daily for its owner even after his death — it's tiny in person and often mobbed, but worth the two minutes.

What to do in Shibuya

  • Experience the crossing from street level and from above.
  • Shop the youth-fashion department stores like Shibuya 109, the district's iconic multi-floor fashion mall.
  • Explore the side streets around Center Gai and Miyashita Park for cafes, restaurants, and bars.
  • Take in a city view from Shibuya Sky or one of the newer rooftop observation decks.

Harajuku

A short walk or one train stop from Shibuya, Harajuku is the center of Tokyo's youth and street fashion. Takeshita Street is its famously colorful, crowded pedestrian lane packed with quirky shops, crepe stands, and whatever trend is peaking that season — it's genuinely narrow, so expect shoulder-to-shoulder crowds on weekends. Just beyond, Omotesando offers a completely different register: a wide, tree-lined boulevard of designer boutiques and architecture from name-brand international architects, more Champs-Élysées than teen fashion strip — flagship stores from Prada, Dior, and a rotating cast of Japanese and international designers occupy buildings by well-known architects, and even if shopping isn't the point, the street itself is worth a slow walk for the architecture alone. The side alley of Ura-Harajuku (behind the main street) is where independent boutiques and vintage shops cluster, a better bet than Takeshita Street itself if crowds aren't your thing.

Meiji Shrine

The contrast that makes this area special: right beside busy Harajuku lies Meiji Shrine, set in a tranquil forest of some 120,000 trees donated from across Japan when it was built. The wooded approach and grand torii gates create one of the most peaceful spots in central Tokyo — a perfect counterpoint to the surrounding bustle. Don't skip it. Adjacent Yoyogi Park is worth a wander too, especially on a weekend when street performers, musicians, and picnicking locals turn it into one of the best people-watching spots in the city.

How to combine them

A natural plan: start with the calm of Meiji Shrine and Yoyogi Park in the morning before the crowds build, wander Harajuku (Takeshita Street and Omotesando), then end in Shibuya for the crossing and an evening out — dinner in the side streets, then the crossing again after dark, when the neon signage makes it a genuinely different sight than the daytime version. It's an easy, walkable progression from serene to electric, and showcases Tokyo's range in a single day. The whole loop is also a reasonable base for your stay: Shibuya in particular is well-connected and worth checking for a hotel if you want nightlife and transit links over old-Tokyo atmosphere. (This article contains affiliate links — if you book through them we earn a small commission at no extra cost to you.)

Practical tips

  • Weekends are extremely crowded in Harajuku and at the crossing — go early or on a weekday if you can, especially for photos.
  • It's all walkable, but the JR Yamanote line connects the stations if you tire.
  • Great area for people-watching and street food (just don't eat while walking) — Takeshita Street's rainbow cotton candy and crepe stands are the classic photo-ops.
  • Meiji Shrine is free to enter, though the inner garden carries a small fee.

Where to eat

Shibuya's side streets hide far better food than the main crossing area suggests — Nonbei Yokocho ("Drunkard's Alley"), a tiny cluster of postwar-era bars and yakitori counters tucked under the train tracks near Shibuya Station, is worth seeking out for something more local than the chain restaurants facing the crossing. Harajuku leans casual and photogenic: beyond the Takeshita Street crepe stands, the side streets around Cat Street (between Harajuku and Omotesando) have a good concentration of cafes if you want to sit down rather than eat on the move — remember, eating while walking is generally frowned on in Japan, so a bench in Yoyogi Park or a cafe seat is the better call than strolling with a crepe in hand.
excerpt: Youthful, fashionable, and endlessly walkable — here is what to do in Tokyo's Shibuya and Harajuku districts, from the famous crossing to Meiji Shrine.

title: Asakusa & Old Tokyo Area Guide
content:
Asakusa is where Tokyo holds onto its past — a district of temples, traditional shops, and old-town atmosphere on the city's northeast side. It's the best place to feel historic Tokyo, and a favorite base for travelers who prefer charm and value over glitz. Here's what to do.

Senso-ji

The centerpiece is Senso-ji, Tokyo's oldest temple, founded in the year 645 according to temple tradition and rebuilt after WWII bombing destroyed the original structure. You enter through the iconic Kaminarimon ("Thunder Gate") with its giant red lantern, then walk the Nakamise shopping street — nearly 90 stalls lined up over roughly 250 meters, selling traditional snacks and souvenirs — up to the grand temple hall and its five-story pagoda. Go early in the morning, ideally before 8am, to experience it before the tour groups arrive; the temple grounds themselves never close, so an early or after-dark visit shows a genuinely different, much quieter side of the same place.

Around the temple

  • Nakamise Street: great for street snacks — try ningyo-yaki (small cakes shaped like temple landmarks) or freshly cooked senbei rice crackers — and traditional souvenirs like folding fans and yukata.
  • Backstreets: wander beyond the main drag, particularly Denboin-dori, for craft shops, old-style eateries, and a noticeably quieter feel than the crowded temple approach.
  • Sumida River: nearby for riverside walks and boat cruises — a water bus runs from Asakusa down to Odaiba, a scenic and relaxed way to see a different stretch of Tokyo.
  • Rickshaw rides: a fun, if touristy and pricier, way to tour the old streets with a guide who narrates as you go.
  • Kimono rental: popular here for strolling the traditional setting in style — same-day rental-and-return shops cluster around the temple approach, no reservation always required though booking ahead guarantees your size and style.

Tokyo Skytree nearby

Just across the river from Asakusa rises Tokyo Skytree, at 634 meters one of the world's tallest towers, with two observation decks, extensive shopping at its base (Tokyo Solamachi), and an aquarium. It's an easy add-on to an Asakusa visit and offers sweeping views, especially near sunset when the city lights start coming on. On the way, look for the Asahi Beer Hall's gold "Flamme d'Or" sculpture across the river — an odd, unmissable piece of Tokyo architecture locals have nicknamed after its resemblance to a certain bodily object, and a fun photo stop either way.

Why stay here

Asakusa is a popular base for first-timers who want traditional atmosphere and often better value than the western hubs — it's genuinely worth comparing hotel prices here against Shinjuku or Shibuya for the same trip dates. (This article contains affiliate links — if you book through them we earn a small commission at no extra cost to you.) The trade-off is that it sits on the eastern side, so reaching Shibuya/Shinjuku takes a bit longer — typically 25-35 minutes by subway — but it's still an easy train ride, and waking up near Senso-ji, with the morning quiet before the crowds, has its own magic that the western hubs can't offer.

Practical tips

  • Visit Senso-ji early or in the evening (the lit-up temple at night is beautiful and uncrowded).
  • Combine Asakusa and Skytree into one easy half-day, crossing via the Azumabashi bridge.
  • The area is walkable and well connected by subway (Ginza and Asakusa lines) and the Tsukuba Express.
  • Carry cash for the small traditional shops along Nakamise and the backstreets — many don't take cards.

Where to eat

Beyond Nakamise's grab-and-go snacks, Asakusa has some of Tokyo's most respected old-school restaurants for tempura and unagi (grilled eel), several running for generations out of the same modest storefronts — a contrast to the flashier dining scenes in Shibuya or Ginza. The backstreets west of the temple (Hoppy Street, named for a beer substitute popular with an older postwar generation) are lined with casual, cash-only izakaya serving grilled skewers and cheap drinks — an atmospheric, unpretentious place for an evening that feels a world away from Shinjuku's neon version of a night out.

A neighborhood that survived

Much of what makes Asakusa feel different from the rest of Tokyo is simply that it's older: the area was the city's main entertainment and theater district for centuries before Shinjuku and Shibuya existed in any recognizable form, and while the 1923 earthquake and WWII bombing destroyed most of the original buildings (Senso-ji included), the street layout and small-shop character were rebuilt close to how they'd always been, rather than redeveloped into the high-rise districts that now define central Tokyo.

Bottom line

For old-Tokyo atmosphere — temples, traditional shops, and a slower pace — Asakusa is unmatched in the city. Pair it with the modern spectacle of Skytree next door, and you've got one of Tokyo's most rewarding and characterful areas.
excerpt: Asakusa is Tokyo's most traditional district, home to Senso-ji temple and old-town charm. Here is what to see, eat, and why it is worth basing here.

title: Gion & Higashiyama Area Guide (Kyoto)
content:
The eastern districts of Gion and Higashiyama are the postcard Kyoto — preserved wooden streets, major temples, and the historic geisha quarter, all walkable together along the base of the eastern hills. This is where most first-timers fall in love with the city, and where a single day on foot can feel like stepping back centuries. Here's how to explore it.

Higashiyama's old streets

The Higashiyama district preserves the atmosphere of old Kyoto better than anywhere else in the city. The sloping stone lanes of Ninenzaka and Sannenzaka are lined with traditional wooden machiya shops, teahouses, craft stores, and street-food and souvenir stalls, climbing gently toward Kiyomizu-dera. Wandering these streets — ideally early in the morning before the crowds and tour groups arrive — is one of Kyoto's great pleasures, all the more so if you spot visitors in rented kimono adding to the timeless scene. Stop for matcha soft-serve, pickles, or a craft souvenir as you go.

Kiyomizu-dera

At the top of the slope sits Kiyomizu-dera, a magnificent wooden temple built into the hillside, famous for its enormous viewing veranda that juts out over the slope on tall wooden pillars (built without nails), offering sweeping views over Kyoto. It's spectacular in cherry blossom and autumn seasons, when the hillside blazes with color, and special evening illuminations are held in peak periods. The approach through the old streets makes the visit doubly rewarding — the journey is as memorable as the destination. A first-trip essential.

Gion, the geisha district

Gion is Kyoto's historic geisha quarter, full of traditional wooden machiya houses, exclusive teahouses (ochaya), and lantern-lit lanes that are especially atmospheric in the evening. The famous Hanamikoji street is its heart, lined with preserved buildings and high-end restaurants. If you're lucky, you may glimpse a geiko (Kyoto's word for a geisha) or a maiko (an apprentice) gliding to an evening appointment in full traditional dress — a fleeting, magical sight.

Gion etiquette

Be respectful: do not chase, block, surround, or grab at geiko or maiko — there have been real problems with tourists harassing them, and some private streets now restrict or ban photography entirely, with fines posted. They are working professionals hurrying to appointments, not tourist attractions. Quiet, courteous observation from a respectful distance is the only acceptable way, and following the posted rules keeps these streets open and welcoming.

More to see nearby

  • Yasaka Shrine: a colorful, lively shrine linking Gion and Higashiyama, beautiful when its lanterns are lit at night and a hub during festivals.
  • Maruyama Park: a popular green space behind Yasaka Shrine, one of Kyoto's most famous cherry-blossom viewing spots.
  • Kodai-ji: an elegant temple with gardens and seasonal night illuminations, plus other quieter temples dotted through the hills.
  • Kennin-ji: Kyoto's oldest Zen temple, near Gion, with striking painted screens and ceiling dragons.
  • Shirakawa area: a quieter, exceptionally pretty canal-side stretch of Gion, lined with willows and traditional restaurants.

How to do it

A great plan strings the area together on foot: start early at Kiyomizu-dera before the crowds, walk down through Sannenzaka and Ninenzaka, continue through the Higashiyama temples and Yasaka Shrine into Maruyama Park, and end in Gion as evening falls — for a stroll down Hanamikoji and Shirakawa, then dinner along the nearby riverside Pontocho Alley. It's a walkable, full day that captures Kyoto's most beautiful side from morning light to lantern-lit dusk. Wear comfortable shoes for the slopes and stone paths.

Why stay here

Staying in Gion or Higashiyama puts you right amid the charm and within walking distance of major temples, so you can enjoy the old streets in the quiet early mornings and evenings when day-trippers have gone. It can be pricier and busier during the day, but for travelers who came to Kyoto for old-Japan beauty, there's simply no more atmospheric base — a traditional machiya or ryokan stay here is the icing on the cake, and worth comparing against other Kyoto neighborhoods before you book. (This article contains affiliate links — if you book through them we earn a small commission at no extra cost to you.)

Where to eat

Gion and Higashiyama run from tourist-friendly to genuinely exclusive. Pontocho Alley, the narrow lantern-lit lane along the Kamo River just west of Gion, has everything from affordable yakitori counters to riverside kaiseki restaurants with summer terrace seating (kawadoko) overlooking the water — a good stretch to simply walk and pick something that looks right rather than plan in advance. The area's traditional teahouses and ochaya, by contrast, are largely invitation-only or require an introduction from a regular customer; a handful of restaurants in Gion offer a more accessible taste of kaiseki-style dining without that barrier, worth booking a few days ahead if a special dinner is part of the plan. For something simpler, the tea shops and dessert counters near Yasaka Shrine serve matcha parfaits and warabimochi that make a good mid-walk break between temples.
excerpt: Gion and Higashiyama are Kyoto's most atmospheric districts — preserved streets, major temples, and the geisha quarter. Here is what to see and eat.

title: Arashiyama Area Guide (Kyoto)
content:
Arashiyama, on Kyoto's western edge, is a district of natural beauty — a famous bamboo grove, a scenic river, important temples, and a hillside monkey park. It has a relaxed, almost resort-like feel, especially once the day crowds thin in the late afternoon and evening. It's one of Kyoto's most rewarding half-days, and a refreshing change of scene from the temple-dense eastern districts. Here's what to see and how to do it.

The Bamboo Grove

The signature sight is the Arashiyama Bamboo Grove, a path winding through towering stalks of bamboo that filter the sunlight into something soft and otherworldly. It's short — you can walk it in fifteen minutes — but genuinely striking and one of Japan's most photographed spots. The catch is its popularity: midday can be shoulder-to-shoulder, so go early in the morning (ideally right after sunrise) to experience the grove in relative peace, with the light at its most beautiful and the crowds still thin.

Tenryu-ji

Right beside the bamboo grove sits Tenryu-ji, one of Kyoto's most important Zen temples and a UNESCO World Heritage site. Its landscape garden, designed to "borrow" the backdrop of the surrounding hills, is considered among the finest in Japan and has survived largely intact for centuries. The temple pairs naturally with the bamboo walk — in fact, the grove's most famous stretch runs right along the temple's northern edge — so visiting both together is the obvious move. There's a small entry fee for the garden.

The river and bridge

The Togetsukyo Bridge ("Moon Crossing Bridge") spans the scenic river at the heart of Arashiyama and is the district's central landmark, with forested mountain backdrops that are spectacular in cherry blossom and autumn seasons. You can stroll the riverbanks, rent a rowboat, or take a traditional boat ride; in summer there's even cormorant fishing in the evenings. The whole riverside area is lovely for a relaxed wander, with cafes and shops nearby.

The Monkey Park

A short but steep hike up the hillside (about 20 minutes) leads to the Iwatayama Monkey Park, where over a hundred wild Japanese macaques roam freely and you can enjoy panoramic views over Kyoto from the top. You can buy food to feed the monkeys from inside a screened hut (the roles are reversed — you're in the enclosure, they're free outside). It's a fun, slightly unusual attraction, especially for families and animal lovers; follow the posted rules about not staring at or touching the monkeys.

More to explore

  • Okochi Sanso Villa: a beautiful garden estate (the former home of a film star) with strolling paths, moss gardens, and views, just beyond the bamboo grove; admission includes matcha and a sweet.
  • Temples and shrines: several quieter ones, such as Gio-ji with its moss garden and the rock-strewn Adashino Nenbutsu-ji, dot the area for peaceful visits away from the crowds.
  • Sagano Scenic Railway: a charming old-fashioned sightseeing train that trundles through the scenic river valley (seasonal, and popular in autumn — book ahead).
  • Katsura River boat rides and riverside dining round out a relaxed day.

How to visit

Arashiyama is on the western edge of Kyoto, so it takes a bit longer to reach from the center — but trains and buses connect it conveniently, and the journey is short. Plan a half-day to full day, ideally starting early for the bamboo grove before the crowds. A natural efficient pairing is to combine Arashiyama with Kinkaku-ji (the Golden Pavilion), since both sit on the western/northern side of the city. For those seeking tranquility and natural beauty, staying overnight in an Arashiyama ryokan is a peaceful, scenic alternative to basing in the central districts — you'll have the riverside and grove almost to yourself once the day-trippers leave, and it's worth comparing a stay here against a central Kyoto base if a quieter trip appeals to you. (This article contains affiliate links — if you book through them we earn a small commission at no extra cost to you.) From central Kyoto, the JR Sagano Line and the Randen (Keifuku) tram both reach Arashiyama in 15-25 minutes, and the walk from Arashiyama Station to the bamboo grove is under ten minutes.

Where to eat

Arashiyama's food leans toward what the area is known for: yudofu (simmered tofu) restaurants near Tenryu-ji serve a Buddhist-temple-adjacent specialty in a quiet, traditional setting, and the streets near the station have plenty of casual matcha sweets and soft-serve stands — a genuine local specialty, even though the tea itself is mostly grown in Uji, south of the city, rather than in Arashiyama. Riverside cafes along the Katsura River are pleasant for a slower lunch with a view of the bridge and hills.

Bottom line

Arashiyama blends Kyoto's natural beauty with major cultural sights — the ethereal bamboo grove, the celebrated Tenryu-ji garden, the scenic river and bridge, and the playful monkey park. Go early, take it slow, and it's one of the most enjoyable and varied days you can have in the city.
excerpt: Kyoto's Arashiyama district offers a famous bamboo grove, riverside scenery, temples, and a monkey park. Here is how to visit and where to eat.
